23.text: Material Conditions. — The material conditions of life of assistants in

24.text: the camp of a master vary according to the quality of their work and the

25.text: size of the herd in the care of which they help. If the assistant has some

26.text: reindeer of his own, they are joined to the herd of the camp, and stay there

27.text: until the separation. In most cases, however, the assistants receive from the

28.text: herd of the master at least the daily food for their families. Their tents are

29.text: pitched in the camp among the “rear houses,” and at most slaughterings all

30.text: the houses of the camp receive one slaughtered reindeer each. Of course, the

31.text: front house receives one of the best, perhaps some large buck or a fat barren

32.text: doe; while the last of the rear houses may receive only a lean fawn hardly one

33.text: year old. This depends also on the position of the assistant in the camp. If the

34.text: master is contented with the work of the assistant, he would not presume to feed

35.text: his family with poor meat. In case the number of slaughtered animals does not

36.text: correspond to the number of houses, each house receives its part of the meat.

37.text: The question of clothing and of material for the tent-covering is decided by

38.text: these slaughterings, because the women of each house take the skins of their

39.text: respective animals, and may use them at will for any wants of their family.

40.text: Tea, sugar, tobacco, iron, and other articles bought from traders, are

41.text: acquired by the assistants, as well as by the masters, quite independently; for
